blocks.title: What a provider website is, and how one program runs hundreds
blocks.subtitle: A rental company gets its own public site. We build and run every one of them.

blocks.title: Why one program instead of one copy per company?
blocks.lede: Start with what the whole thing is, before any of its parts.

blocks.title: Who actually answers, when everyone arrives at once?
The three layers a visit passes through
blocks.note: Most visits stop at the edge and never reach the application at all.

blocks.title: What happens between typing an address and seeing a page

steps.title: The address is looked up
steps.text: Every company address points at the same edge.

steps.title: The edge checks its cache
steps.text: If the page is ready, it goes straight back.

steps.title: The connection is secured
steps.text: Encryption is agreed before anything else is sent.

steps.title: The tenant is worked out
steps.text: The address is matched to exactly one company.

steps.title: The page is built or reused
steps.text: A recent copy is reused wherever one exists.

steps.title: Live details are fetched
steps.text: Availability and prices are never served from cache.

blocks.note: An address matching no company gets a plain error, never somebody else's site.

blocks.title: Method
items: The claim that most visits stop at the edge is a design target for the full-page cache, not a figure observed in production.
The planning target agreed for the first two years is 500 or more company sites.
This document explains what the thing is. The choice between the five candidate designs, and the scores behind it, is a separate document written for the team that has to build it.
Tenant: one company's site, keyed by website_id and provider_id.
Host header: the web address, as the program actually receives it.
ACME / SNI: how thousands of addresses share a handful of machines.
Read model: data the site reads from RentOS and never writes.
